title: Nobody Is a Good Listener
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Having just defended his dissertation on how principals and teachers talk with one another, Rod Naquin argues that good leadership talk is a constant, mostly invisible process of reading the person in front of you and adjusting. He explains that conversation is hard to see because we are inside it, pointing to interactive alignment, the unconscious matching of words, speed and posture, and to research by Huang and colleagues showing that people who ask more follow-up questions are liked more but do not realise it. Drawing on Kluger and Itzchakov's review, he separates listening into the listener's internal state, visible behaviours and the speaker's sense of being heard, with the last mattering most for outcomes. A study cited shows that 42 percent of the variance in perceived listening came from the specific pairing of two people. He closes with a weekly talk move for instructional leaders.
points: Conversation is pervasive, which makes it hard to notice in ourselves, and people align unconsciously with each other's words, pace and posture.
Asking follow-up questions makes people like you more, yet participants did not realise this or track how many questions they asked.
Listening has three layers, the listener's internal state, their visible behaviours and the speaker's feeling of being heard, and outcomes track the third.
About 42 percent of how well someone feels listened to comes from the specific pair of people, so listening is mostly a property of the relationship.
The suggested talk move is to ask a teacher to walk you through what something was actually like, then stay quiet a few seconds longer than is comfortable.
quotes: Good leadership talk isn’t a style a principal masters once. It’s a constant, mostly invisible process of reading the person in front of you and adjusting
Ubiquitous means you’d find it anywhere you looked. Pervasive means it’s soaked so completely into everything that you stop seeing it at all.
But when participants were asked to predict this, they couldn’t. They didn’t realize questions would help, and they didn’t track how many they were asking.
Nod, paraphrase, repeat back: you can do all three and still leave someone feeling unheard.
Trust, job satisfaction, creativity, lower burnout: all of these track closely with whether the speaker felt heard, not with what the listener did or intended.
Put plainly: listening is mostly a property of the pair, not the person. Beth isn’t a good listener. Beth is a good listener to Alan.
Not “am I a good listener?” but “what happens in the space between me and this teacher?
Instead, ask: “Can you walk me through what that was actually like?” Then stay quiet a few seconds longer than feels comfortable.
